meta.title: Who really said "All truths are easy to understand once they are discovered; the point is to discover them"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Attributed to Galileo, but nobody can point to a Galileo text. The oldest citation anyone offers is a 1999 business book.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'All truths are easy to understand once they are discovered; the point is to discover them'?
meta.ogDescription: Wikiquote files it under “Attributed” — its unsourced list — citing a 1999 business book. Three Galileo works searched, no match.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely printed as Galileo’s, and it does sound like him. But no primary source has been produced. Wikiquote keeps it in its “Attributed” section ↗ — the list for lines credited to him without a source — and offers a single citation: a 1999 business-inspiration book. We searched three of his major works ourselves and found nothing like it.

source.heading: What we could and could not find

docMeta.dd: Attributed — its section for unsourced credits, distinct from the “Misattributed” section it also keeps for Galileo
Melissa Giovagnoli, Angels in the Workplace (San Francisco: Jossey-Bass, 1999)
Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi; Two New Sciences; Drake’s Discoveries and Opinions of Galileo

source.excerpt: All truths are easy to understand once they are discovered; the point is to discover them.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line under Attributed ↗, not under Quotes, and its sole citation is Angels in the Workplace: Stories and Inspirations for Creating a New World of Work (1999) by Melissa Giovagnoli. Wikiquote keeps a separate Misattributed section for Galileo, and this line is not in it.

Italian Wikiquote ↗ is no better anchored: it carries the line as “Tutte le verità sono facili da capire una volta che sono state rivelate” and cites Il libro della scienza (Gribaudo, 2018) — an Italian translation of a modern popular-science book, not a Galileo text.

We searched the primary works rather than trusting a quotation site. The complete Italian Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi ↗ contains no sentence pairing truth with ease of understanding; neither does the 1914 Crew and de Salvio translation of Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences ↗, nor Drake’s Discoveries and Opinions of Galileo ↗.

The 1999 book is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗, published by Jossey-Bass in San Francisco. Its text is access-restricted, so we could not read its pages — we can only report that Wikiquote points there, and that the documented trail stops in 1999 rather than in the seventeenth century.
source.excerptNote: We print the line as it circulates. We have not found it in anything Galileo wrote, so there is no fuller original context to show.
source.rightsNote: We are not asserting a rights status. Public-domain status would depend on a specific pre-1931 work containing this wording, and we have not found any work containing it at all. The oldest text anyone points to is from 1999 and is in copyright; whether the sentence originated there, in an earlier paraphrase, or with Galileo himself is exactly what we could not establish.

author.name: Galileo Galilei
author.heading: About Galileo Galilei
author.metaLine: 1564–1642 · Italian astronomer, physicist, engineer and polymath
author.bio: Galileo Galilei was born in Pisa in 1564 and has been called the father of observational astronomy, of classical physics and of the scientific method. He turned a telescope on Jupiter and found moons, argued for the Copernican system in the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632), was condemned for it in 1633 and spent the rest of his life under house arrest, writing the Two New Sciences there. He is also one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for crisp sentences about truth and discovery that nobody can find in his books.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source located. Earliest citation we could document: Wikiquote, “Galileo Galilei,” Attributed ↗, which cites Melissa Giovagnoli, Angels in the Workplace: Stories and Inspirations for Creating a New World of Work (San Francisco: Jossey-Bass, 1999). The line does not appear in the Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi, in Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences (trans. Crew and de Salvio, 1914), or in Stillman Drake, trans., Discoveries and Opinions of Galileo (1957).
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘All truths are easy to understand once they are discovered; the point is to discover them’?” Last verified 23 Aug 2026.

copyAttribution: "All truths are easy to understand once they are discovered; the point is to discover them." — Attributed to Galileo Galilei, but with no known primary source. Wikiquote lists it among his unsourced attributed quotations, citing only Melissa Giovagnoli, Angels in the Workplace (San Francisco: Jossey-Bass, 1999). We found no match in the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, in Two New Sciences, or in Stillman Drake's Discoveries and Opinions of Galileo.

misattribution.heading: What gets claimed for it
misattribution.intro: Nothing here is proven wrong. What is wrong is the confidence with which the line gets sourced.

items.why: The line is sometimes said to come from the Dialogue, as an exchange between Salviati and Sagredo. We searched the complete Italian text ↗ and found no such passage — no sentence there pairs truth with ease of understanding.
Aggregators print the line as Galileo’s with no work, date or page. Wikiquote is more careful ↗ and files it as unsourced.

misattribution.truthLine: It may well be his. On the evidence available, nobody can show that it is — and the specialist entry says so plainly ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The sentiment is a real one in Galileo’s world: that a demonstration, once made, looks obvious, and that the whole difficulty lies in getting there first. He wrote things close to it in spirit. What he does not appear to have written is this sentence.

That gap is ordinary. Galileo is one of the names lines drift toward — four separate quotations on Wikiquote’s Galileo page are filed as outright misattributions, including “Eppur si muove” and “Measure what is measurable.” A crisp aphorism about discovery is exactly the shape that ends up under his name.
detailsBody: Wikiquote draws a line most quotation sites do not: Attributed means credited to him without a source, while Misattributed means positively traced to someone else. This sentence sits in the first list, which is why we call it attributed rather than disputed. Asserting it is not his would claim more than the evidence supports, in the opposite direction.

We searched three works: the Dialogue in Italian, Two New Sciences in the 1914 English translation, and Drake’s collection of the shorter pieces. That is not everything Galileo wrote — Favaro’s national edition runs to twenty volumes ↗, published between 1890 and 1909 and containing a great deal of correspondence — so absence from three books is a real result but not a verdict.
context.pull: It may well be his. Nobody has yet shown that it is.

sourcesVerified.claim: English Wikiquote lists 'All truths are easy to understand once they are discovered; the point is to discover them' in its Attributed section for Galileo Galilei, citing Melissa Giovagnoli, Angels in the workplace (1999); the page also keeps a separate Misattributed section that does not contain this line.

Italian Wikiquote carries 'Tutte le verita sono facili da capire una volta che sono state rivelate. Il difficile e scoprirle' sourced to Il libro della scienza (Gribaudo, 2018), a translated popular-science book.
The complete Italian text of Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi (Einaudi, ed. Libero Sosio) contains no sentence pairing 'verita' with 'facil-' and no equivalent of the quoted line.
The 1914 Crew and de Salvio translation of Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences contains no phrase 'once they are discovered', 'the point is to discover' or 'truths are ... easy'.
Stillman Drake's Discoveries and Opinions of Galileo (1957) contains no phrase 'once they are discovered', 'the point is to discover' or 'truths are ... easy'.

The Internet Archive catalogues Melissa Giovagnoli, Angels in the workplace: stories and inspirations for creating a new world of work (San Francisco: Jossey-Bass, 1999); the item is access-restricted so its text could not be searched.
The Italian Wikisource index of Le opere di Galileo Galilei (Favaro) lists volumes I through XX and gives the publication years as 1890/1909.
